source.title: Transmitting Misalignment with Subliminal Learning via Paraphrasing
source.authors: Matthew Bozoukov; Taywon Min; CallumMcDougall; J Rosser

record.tranche_reason: Tests subliminal trait transfer in a new setting: filtered, paraphrased natural-language datasets rather than the original number-sequence setup; it also tests transfer across two model families.
record.gate_note: The post reports behavioral outcomes for animal preference and misalignment, including cross-model transfer and divergence-based sample selection. Cited findings from other work and illustrative individual responses are not recorded as separate rows. Figures 1 and 2 are referenced but their numerical values are not present in the supplied text; the post explicitly describes the direction of the results.
record.test_reason: The post applies the subliminal-learning recipe in a new setting: teacher-paraphrased Alpaca and MathQA data, filtered for the trait. It reports student trait rates for animal preference and emergent misalignment, a divergence-token selection result, and a cross-family Qwen/Llama test.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. Add the authors' hypothesis that Llama models absorb subtle biases more readily, while Qwen models are stronger teachers but less susceptible. Add their claim that paraphrase-based tampering would be hard to detect. They also call the divergence and cross-model results preliminary.
record.recipe_differences: Keeps teacher-generated data, filtering, student fine-tuning, and behavioral evaluation, but uses paraphrases of Alpaca and MathQA rather than the original random-number generation setup; also tests divergence-based sample selection.
record.method_sensitivity: Cross-model transfer varies by teacher-student direction. Selecting the top 10k samples by divergence-token measures increases the misalignment rate. The post also states that the effect is strongest when overfitting, with a peak around 5–10 epochs.

fits_no_version.finding: A footnote says the effect is strongest when overfitting, peaking around 5–10 epochs. No numbers are given.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Subliminal transmission strength depends on training duration and overfitting.

record.problems: Animal-preference results are described as increases across tested animals but the supplied text does not give their individual numerical values. Cross-model results have no reported rates and are characterized as minimal. No uncertainty estimates are stated.
record.rows_left_out: No separately reported qualifying results were omitted. Individual animal-by-dataset values are not available in the supplied text; R1 and R2 retain the reported aggregate direction for each dataset.

untested.parts: The original data types (number sequences, code, maths chain-of-thought), student families other than Llama in the same-base setting, and teachers given the trait by fine-tuning for animal preference.
Cross-family tests for animal preference; model pairs other than Qwen2.5-7B and Llama-3.1-8B; any numerical rates.
Alignment-relevant traits other than emergent misalignment.
Token entanglement, a steering-vector direction, or a gradient argument. Only divergence-token-based data selection is tested.
Full fine-tuning vs LoRA, other LoRA ranks, and evaluation prompts different from training (only rank 32 LoRA was used).

missing.what: Per-animal base vs student preference rates
Separate misalignment rates for Div Ratio and Div Token selection
Numerical misalignment rates and baselines for both cross-model directions

record.verdict_notes: There is no control student fine-tuned on paraphrases from an unbiased teacher. Any rise in misalignment from fine-tuning itself on paraphrased data is therefore not ruled out. The paraphrased data are semantically related to the original answers, not unrelated like number sequences. Misalignment filtering used a judge threshold of 78 on data averaging about 50 before filtering, so residual semantic misalignment is possible. No uncertainty estimates are given anywhere.

versions.untested_parts: Tests paraphrased Alpaca and MathQA data, not number sequences, code, or maths reasoning as in the claim's examples; cross-model tests cover only the two reported model-family directions.

Tests cross-family transfer between Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct in the misalignment setting only; no broader set of model families or animal-preference cross-base tests are reported.
Tests emergent misalignment only; other alignment-relevant traits are not tested.
Tests selection of paraphrased samples by divergence-token measures; does not establish token entanglement, a steering-vector-like mechanism, or a gradient argument.
No comparison of full fine-tuning with LoRA, other LoRA ranks, or evaluation prompts different from training is reported.

source_check.notes: The record's controls=y overstates things: the only baseline is the pre-fine-tuning model, with no neutral or aligned-teacher paraphrase control, so generic fine-tuning effects on EM aren't excluded. A footnote says the effect peaks when overfitting (5-10 epochs), and training ran 10 epochs. The EM criterion 'misalignment < 30' is given as written and probably means alignment score.

statements.correction: lw:qwAiKvomuAm5ekC4D: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct teacher (system-prompted animal preference) and student (LoRA r32, alpha 64, 10 epochs, 10k samples); paraphrased Alpaca and MathQA, judge filter removes relevance >30; preference for target animal rose for all tested animals vs pre-fine-tuning base model (figure only); no neutral-teacher control; no uncertainty; LessWrong post with code.
statements.problem: Cites R1,R2 from this study, but the visible text never describes it. The Students list leaves out its Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct student. The why-line ('All are preprints') doesn't cover it: it is an informal LessWrong post with no neutral-teacher control and no uncertainty.

statements.correction: lw:qwAiKvomuAm5ekC4D: misaligned Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct teacher (Turner et al.) paraphrases Alpaca; samples with alignment score <78 removed; Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct student EM rate 0.32% to 5.50% (Betley et al. 9 questions, 100 samples each); compared only with the pre-fine-tuning model; no uncertainty.
statements.problem: Cites R3, but the visible text doesn't describe this study. The Carriers and Students lists leave out its paraphrased-Alpaca carrier and its Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct same-base pair.

statements.correction: lw:qwAiKvomuAm5ekC4D: code released; baseline is the pre-fine-tuning model (0.32%); no aligned/neutral-teacher paraphrase control; no capability check; no uncertainty.
statements.problem: The numbers and setup are right. 'With code and controls' is wrong: the only comparison is the model before fine-tuning. No student was trained on aligned or neutral-teacher paraphrases.

statements.correction: lw:qwAiKvomuAm5ekC4D: Betley et al. 9 evaluation questions, 100 samples each; unnamed LLM judge; misaligned = coherence >50 and misalignment <30 (as written).
statements.problem: This study's numbers are right. 'The rows do not state judges or question sets' is partly wrong here: the post names the question set, though the judge is an unnamed LLM.

statements.correction: lw:qwAiKvomuAm5ekC4D: divergent tokens = positions where base model's argmax differs from biased teacher's; top 10k of ~50k paraphrases selected by divergent-token ratio or count; Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct EM rate 5.5% to 7.09%; single run, no uncertainty; authors call it preliminary.
statements.problem: Cites R4, but the visible text doesn't describe this study. This study also defines divergence tokens differently: biased teacher vs base model argmax, not two differently biased teachers.
